package_info.package_name: N/A (Repojacked packages—names vary, e.g., hijacked Go/Swift/PHP packages)
package_info.package_manager: VCS-based (GitHub, used by Go, Swift, PHP package managers)
package_info.why_malicious: The entire package is considered malicious because attackers can take over previously popular repositories via a GitHub namespace retirement bypass, then serve malicious code under trusted package names. This allows attackers to inject arbitrary code into the supply chain, affecting all downstream users who fetch code directly from the hijacked repository. The malicious code is designed to execute automatically upon import or build, exfiltrating sensitive data such as environment variables and private keys to attacker-controlled infrastructure.

execution_context.trigger: import-time or build-time (when the package is fetched and initialized from the hijacked repository)
execution_context.file_location: main source file of the hijacked repository (e.g., main.go, index.php, etc.)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time or build-time, the code accesses the SECRET_TOKEN environment variable, sends its value to a hardcoded attacker-controlled domain via HTTP POST, resulting in credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code automatically executes upon import or build, accesses sensitive environment variables, and exfiltrates their values to an external, attacker-controlled server. This behavior is a hallmark of supply chain attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate open-source packages do not access or transmit secrets or environment variables to third-party servers during import or build processes.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some telemetry or crash reporting libraries may send non-sensitive diagnostic data to vendor servers, but they never transmit secrets or environment variables without explicit user consent.
key_indicators: Automatic execution via Go init() function at import/build time
Access to environment variables unrelated to package functionality
Outbound HTTP POST requests to hardcoded, untrusted domains
No user interaction required for execution

execution_context.trigger: import-time or build-time (when the package is fetched and initialized from the hijacked repository)
execution_context.file_location: main source file or build script of the hijacked repository

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time or build-time, the code reads the user's SSH private key file (~/.ssh/id_rsa) and exfiltrates its contents to a hardcoded attacker-controlled server via HTTP POST, resulting in credential theft.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code reads a highly sensitive file (SSH private key) and transmits its contents to an external server without user knowledge or consent, which is a direct compromise of user credentials.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should never access or transmit user private keys or other sensitive files, especially during import or build time.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate reason for an open-source package to access or exfiltrate SSH private keys or similar sensitive files.
key_indicators: Automatic execution via Go init() function at import/build time
Access to ~/.ssh/id_rsa or other sensitive credential files
Outbound HTTP POST requests to attacker-controlled domains

attack_chain.action: Attacker claims a previously popular GitHub username and creates a repository with the same name as a retired namespace, exploiting a namespace retirement bypass.
attack_chain.leads_to: Allows attacker to serve code under a trusted package name, making it indistinguishable from the original for downstream users.

attack_chain.action: Attacker uploads malicious code to the hijacked repository, embedding code that exfiltrates secrets and sensitive files.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is now available to downstream users who fetch the package.

attack_chain.action: Downstream users or CI systems fetch the package from the hijacked repository via Go, Swift, or PHP package managers, trusting the original package name.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is downloaded and prepared for execution on user systems.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code executes automatically at import or build time, exfiltrating environment variables and sensitive files to attacker infrastructure.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains access to secrets, credentials, or sensitive data from affected systems.

behavioral_signatures: Automatic execution of code on import or build in packages fetched from GitHub repositories with recent ownership changes
Access to environment variables or sensitive files (e.g., ~/.ssh/id_rsa, ~/.aws/credentials) in package initialization code
Outbound network requests to hardcoded or previously unseen domains during package installation, import, or build
file_indicators: Presence of unexpected or new code in main source files (e.g., main.go, index.php) of popular packages after a repository rename or transfer
References to sensitive file paths such as ~/.ssh/id_rsa, ~/.aws/credentials, or other credential stores
Sudden changes in repository commit history, maintainers, or GitHub repository ownership
network_indicators: HTTP/HTTPS POST requests to domains not previously associated with the package (e.g., attacker.com, webhook.site)
Outbound connections to attacker-controlled infrastructure during package import or build
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for packages whose source repository has changed ownership, been renamed, or transferred, especially if the repository was previously popular. Analyze package source code for automatic execution blocks (such as Go init functions or PHP autoloaders) that access environment variables or sensitive files and make outbound network requests. Flag any package that attempts to exfiltrate data to untrusted domains or accesses sensitive files during import or build. Use dependency scanning tools to identify packages fetched directly from GitHub and verify repository ownership and commit history for anomalies.
